I got the solve in decent enough time, but I simply couldn't get a flow going on this one. I'm glad for the folks who enjoyed it, but this was a surprisingly sloggy Sunday puzzle for me. 

I'm always fascinated by how some constructors and I seem to be on exactly the same wavelength, and how other constructors just aren't operating at my frequency (or vice versa, in fairness).

Usually when a constructor places a colorful commonly-used phrase in a grid – one that doesn’t often show up in puzzles – it gets high praise.  Which is what it deserves, because so many such phrases have simply worn out their welcome, and new ones aren’t very easy to come by.

But look at what Peter did today – seven common phrases, all with dash, all so sweetly conversational … and five of them have never shown up in the Times puzzle before.  The other two – I’M OVER HERE and I MISSED YOU have appeared only once before.

That is not only amazing; it elevates the entire puzzle, fills it with interest.

Speaking of newness, how about the theme answers acting as the clues for their clues?  How cool is that?

Plus, it was fun trying to guess the theme answers with as few crosses as possible.

When you add color, newness and fun to the normal pleasure of filling the grid – and you did just that, Peter – created a most gratifying and splendid outing.  This was fabulous, and thank you!

Hah, that was fun! The clues for I’M A BIT CONFUSED and I HAVE NO WORDS are especially clever. Those phrases also represent how I felt before and after the theme clicked. 

Well done, Peter. I eagerly await your next offering ...

Like many high school German students, I had to learn the German folksong "Die Lorelei." Problem was, it isn't really a folk song. The poem was written in 1824 by the prolific poet Heinrich Heine, and the folk-songy tune I learned to sing it to was composed in 1837 by Friedrich Silcher: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1CqdU-mYE8I&list=RD1CqdU-mYE8I&start_radio=1 But Heine's poem has been set by other composers, including Clara Schumann: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uy2O5MxuY70&list=RDuy2O5MxuY70&start_radio=1 (Channeling a bit of the Erlkönig there, Clara?) But looking al this up on YouTube reminded me that there are songs about die Lorelei by Styx: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aFUmaV_gGYE&list=RDaFUmaV_gGYE&start_radio=1 (OK, Boomer, normally I would not post a link like that, but it was shot at Blossom Music Center; for you purists, and those who prefer Dennis, here you go: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7fvPeoT2z00&list=RD7fvPeoT2z00&start_radio=1 ) And by Cocteau Twins: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zV_nrTH5jOc&list=RDzV_nrTH5jOc&start_radio=1 And I'm sure there are others. And that, my friends, is what, with her singing, the Lorelei has done!

A grueling day, reinforcing the seal on our antique refrigerator (been in the family at least 50 years), mopping up melted ice, marveling at icebergs that had mysteriously formed on the interior walls of the fridge instead of in the freezer, measuring, sticking on tape. pulling it off, remeasuring.   

Still, it runs silent, freezes deep, and is the ideal appliance.  I never want another one. and this was a price we were wiling to pay for a fridge far superior to anything that's made now.  It has needed repair only once, a few years ago, and the repairman said if we ever wanted to sell it, to please call him.

Finally it was all done, and what I really,really needed was a really fine puzzle to unwind after a really tense day—and voila, I got one.  

Thank you, Peter, you saved me

This I learned about BAOBABs:

From Wikipedia--
"The tree also grows wild in Sudan in the regions of Darfur and the state of Kordofan. The locals call it gongolaze and use its fruit as food and medicine and use the tree trunks as reservoirs to save water.[citation needed]

"Ecology
Baobabs store water in the trunk (up to 120,000 litres or 32,000 US gallons) to endure harsh drought conditions.[29] All occur in seasonally arid areas, and are deciduous, shedding their leaves during the dry season. Across Africa, the oldest and largest baobabs began to die in the early 21st century, likely from a combination of drought and rising temperatures.[13] The trees appear to become parched, then become dehydrated and unable to support their massive trunks.[14]"
